title: Weight Loss That Lasts
hook: Crash diets win the first month and lose the year. Slow, steady loss built on habits you can actually keep is what stays off.
key_points: Aim for slow, steady loss — small weekly changes beat dramatic drops.
Habits you can sustain outlast any short-term 'diet'.
Crash and fad diets often rebound once you stop, regaining the weight.
Pair better eating with more movement, and get support if you need it.
content_html: The diets that promise to melt weight off fast usually deliver — for about a month. Then the restriction becomes unbearable, old habits return, and the weight comes back, often with interest. The approach that actually sticks is far less dramatic: lose slowly and steadily by changing habits you can live with.
extra_html: The NHS frames lasting weight loss around gradual, sustainable change rather than quick fixes. The reason crash and fad diets disappoint is structural — they depend on extreme restriction nobody maintains, so the moment you stop, the weight rebounds. Steady loss of a modest amount each week, by contrast, gives your routines time to reset. Practically, that means combining better everyday eating with more movement, leaning on small repeatable changes over heroic ones, and getting support — from people around you or a clinician — when you need it. If you have a medical condition or take medication, check with a doctor before starting a weight-loss plan.

related.title: Finding a Healthy Weight
related.hook: BMI is a quick screen, not a verdict. A healthy weight is the range where your risk of disease stays low — and your waistline tells part of the story too.

related.title: Building a Balanced Plate
related.hook: Forget counting every calorie — the simplest healthy-eating tool is a picture of a plate: half produce, a quarter grains, a quarter protein.

related.title: How Much Exercise You Actually Need
related.hook: The headline number is smaller than most people fear: about 150 minutes of moderate activity a week — roughly 20-some minutes a day — moves the needle on your health.

flashcards.prompt: Why do crash diets tend to fail in the long run?
flashcards.back_html: They rely on extreme, short-term restriction you can't keep up, so the weight often comes back once you stop. Slow, steady loss built on sustainable habits is what actually lasts.

flashcards.prompt: What's the more reliable approach to lasting weight loss?

choices.text: Gradual loss through habits you can maintain over time
The fastest possible drop using a very restrictive diet
Skipping meals entirely until you reach your goal

flashcards.explanation_html: The NHS emphasizes steady, gradual loss through sustainable changes to eating and activity, rather than rapid crash dieting that tends to rebound.
